d: Ratio of signal power to noise power, usually in dB. Sets detectability and the precision of every estimate in the course.
The raw, real-valued echo signal around the transducer centre frequency, sampled above its Nyquist rate (typically 4× the centre frequency or more), before demodulation to IQ.
Complex signal obtained by mixing RF down to baseband and low-pass filtering; I is the real part, Q the imaginary part.
An O(N log N) algorithm that computes the DFT.
The fast algorithm for the inverse DFT.
Maps N samples to N complex frequency coefficients; the finite, sampled version of the Fourier transform.
Fourier transform of an infinite discrete-time sequence; a continuous, 2π-periodic function of frequency. The DFT samples it.
Fourier transforms of short, windowed, usually overlapping segments, giving a time–frequency picture.
A system whose response to a weighted sum of inputs is the same weighted sum of the responses, and whose behaviour does not change over time; fully described by its impulse response.
A digital filter whose impulse response has finite length; always stable and can have exactly linear phase.
A recursive digital filter whose impulse response never ends; cheaper than FIR for sharp responses but can be unstable and has nonlinear phase.
Passes frequencies below a cut-off and attenuates those above.
Stability criterion: every bounded input gives a bounded output. For LTI systems, the impulse response must be absolutely summable.
Distribution of a random signal's power over frequency; the Fourier transform of its autocorrelation.
Width of an ideal rectangular filter passing the same white-noise power as a given window or filter.
The zero-frequency (mean) component of a signal.
A random process whose mean is constant and whose covariance depends only on the time difference.
A multiplier-free filter structure used for large decimation factors.
Model in which each sample is a weighted sum of past samples plus white noise; used for spectral estimation and prediction.
Slepian tapers that maximize energy concentration in a band; the windows of the multitaper method.
Analog low-pass filter before the ADC that removes content above half the sampling rate.
Number of transmit events per second; sets the Doppler Nyquist limit and the maximum imaging depth.
Time between transmit events; 1/PRF.
Bandwidth divided by centre frequency, often at −6 dB.
Width of the frequency band a signal or system occupies, usually defined at −3 or −6 dB.
A pulse whose instantaneous frequency sweeps linearly in time; compressed by a matched filter.
Code duration times bandwidth; approximately the compression ratio, and the SNR gain of pulse compression relative to a short pulse of equal peak amplitude.
Highest sidelobe relative to the main lobe, in dB, for a beam pattern or a compressed pulse.
Energy in all sidelobes relative to the main-lobe energy, in dB.
Contrast or harmonic pulse sequence that combines transmits of different amplitudes so linear echoes cancel.
Two transmits of opposite polarity are summed so linear echoes cancel and even harmonics remain.
Multi-pulse sequence combining amplitude and phase changes to isolate nonlinear microbubble echoes.
Factorization A = UΣVᴴ into orthonormal bases and non-negative singular values; the tool behind clutter filtering, conditioning and regularization.
Regularization that keeps only the largest singular values when inverting.
Finding the directions of largest variance; the SVD of centred data.
Factorization into an orthonormal Q and an upper-triangular R; a stable way to solve least squares.
Choosing parameters that minimize the sum of squared residuals.
Lower bound on the variance of any unbiased estimator, given by the inverse Fisher information.
The parameter value that makes the observed data most probable.
Estimate that maximizes the posterior: likelihood times prior.
Average squared estimation error; variance plus squared bias.
Square root of the MSE, in the units of the quantity.
Estimator that minimizes the expected squared error; the posterior mean.
Signal energy divided by noise power spectral density; sets the CRLB for delay and localization.
Cross-correlation of mean-removed signals divided by the square root of the product of their energies, so it lies between −1 and 1; the standard similarity measure for speckle tracking.
Regularizer equal to the sum of gradient magnitudes; it favours piecewise-constant images with sharp edges.
Rule for choosing a regularization parameter by predicting held-out error without re-fitting.
Proximal-gradient method for L1-regularized problems: a gradient step, then soft thresholding.
ISTA with Nesterov momentum; the objective error falls as O(1/k²) instead of ISTA's O(1/k) (Beck & Teboulle 2009).
Krylov method that solves least squares without forming AᴴA; stopping early acts as regularization.
Splits an optimization into simpler sub-problems that are solved in turn and tied together by dual variables.
Solves non-quadratic fitting problems as a sequence of weighted least-squares problems.
Iterative minimization by stepping against the gradient.
Damped Gauss–Newton method that moves between Gauss–Newton and gradient descent.
Gradient descent using noisy gradients from random subsets of the data.
Estimates a sound-speed map by fitting full simulated waveforms to measured data.
Eigen-analysis of the inter-element response matrix; for well-resolved point scatterers, each strong singular vector focuses on one scatterer.
Signal power divided by interference plus noise power; the figure of merit for adaptive beamformers.
Result that a sample covariance from about 2N snapshots costs roughly 3 dB of SINR in an N-element adaptive beamformer.
Adaptive beamforming that inverts the measured sample covariance matrix.
Beamforming by delaying each channel to align echoes from a point, then summing; the reference method.
Image of a single point scatterer; sets resolution and sidelobe levels.
Width of a peak at half its maximum (−6 dB for amplitude); the usual resolution measure.
Adaptive beamformer that minimizes output power while keeping unit gain in the look direction.
Another name for the minimum-variance (Capon) beamformer.
MV beamformer whose weights are projected onto the signal subspace of the covariance matrix.
Ratio of coherent to incoherent energy across the aperture; used as a pixel weight that suppresses clutter.
Coherence factor that counts low spatial frequencies across the aperture as coherent energy.
Weight based on the spread of channel phases instead of amplitudes.
Weight based on the agreement of channel signs (polarity).
Image formed from the spatial coherence of channel signals at small element lags, not from echo amplitude.

For diffuse scatterers, the spatial coherence of echoes across the receive aperture is the Fourier transform of the insonified intensity distribution; at the transmit focus it equals the autocorrelation of the transmit apodization.
Nonlinear beamformer that sums products of channel pairs after delay.
Suppresses incoherent clutter by predicting each channel from its neighbours in the frequency–space domain.
Model-based beamformer that fits channel data with a set of modelled wavefronts and keeps only the components from the region of interest.
Image region selected for measurement or processing.
Difference of mean intensities inside and outside a target, divided by a noise or speckle measure.
Ratio of mean intensities inside and outside a target, usually in dB.
1 minus the overlap of the intensity distributions inside and outside a target; ranges from 0 to 1 and is unchanged by monotonic transforms such as log compression (Rodriguez-Molares et al. 2020).
Area shared by the inside and outside intensity distributions; gCNR = 1 − OVL.

f: Plane-wave Imaging Challenge in Medical Ultrasound
d: IUS 2016 challenge that released shared plane-wave datasets and metrics for comparing beamformers.
Axial range over which a focused beam stays near its focal width.
Imaging with unfocused plane-wave transmits, often at several angles that are compounded.
Imaging that focuses every pixel by combining many single-element or small-aperture transmits.
2D array whose elements are addressed through whole rows or whole columns (e.g. rows on transmit, columns on receive), so N+N channels serve an N×N aperture.
Propagation speed of sound in the medium; about 1540 m/s is the usual soft-tissue assumption.

f: computed ultrasound tomography in echo mode
d: Estimates a sound-speed map from phase shifts between images beamformed at different transmit/receive angles.

CUTE refinement (Stähli et al. 2020) that compares transmit/receive angle pairs sharing the same mid-angle; these sample the same k-space region, so their speckle stays correlated and the phase difference reflects sound-speed error.

f: retrospective encoding for conventional ultrasound sequences
d: Decodes the transmit sequence from channel data so any transmit set can be refocused like synthetic aperture data.
Super-resolution imaging that localizes and tracks individual microbubbles over many frames.
Open ULM benchmark (Heiles et al. 2022) with shared data and metrics.
Resolution measure from the correlation of two independent half-images over rings in k-space.
Learned model built from layers of weighted sums and nonlinearities.
Transmission without pulses; gives Doppler without range resolution.
Doppler mode with pulsed transmission and a range gate.
Image of the Doppler signal power after clutter filtering, regardless of velocity.
Imaging of tissue displacement caused by a long focused push pulse.
Measures shear-wave speed to estimate tissue stiffness.
Arrival-time method, e.g. estimating shear-wave speed from arrival times at several lateral positions.
Imaging with gas microbubble contrast agents.

f: time–intensity curve (contrast); cranial thermal index (acoustic output)
d: Two meanings. In contrast imaging (Module 28): echo intensity in an ROI versus time after injection. In acoustic output (Modules 22, 36): the cranial-bone thermal index, the TI with bone at the skin surface, as in transcranial scanning.

Time at which a curve peaks: in contrast imaging, from arrival or injection to the time–intensity-curve maximum; in shear-wave elastography (Module 30), when the displacement peaks at each lateral position.
Mean time contrast takes to pass through the tissue; a perfusion parameter from the TIC.
Microbubble signal relative to the residual tissue signal after contrast processing, in dB.
A lipid commonly used in microbubble shells.
Estimates tissue properties (attenuation, backscatter, scatterer size, speed of sound) as numbers rather than images.
Backscattered power per unit volume, solid angle and incident intensity; frequency dependence carries scatterer size.
Scatterer size estimated by fitting a form factor to the frequency dependence of the BSC.
Attenuation estimate from the log ratio of power spectra from two depths in a homogeneous region; its slope versus frequency, divided by 4Δz, gives the attenuation coefficient slope (Np/cm/MHz).
The standard piezoelectric ceramic for medical transducers.
Relaxor single crystal with higher coupling than PZT; used in wide-band probes.
Flexible piezoelectric polymer with low impedance; common in hydrophones.
Equivalent circuit of a thickness-mode transducer as an acoustic transmission line coupled to an electrical port.
Lumped equivalent circuit (static capacitance in parallel with a series RLC) of a resonator near resonance.
Two-port representation that chains layers by matrix multiplication.
Unit of acoustic impedance, 10⁶ kg/(m²·s). Soft tissue is about 1.5 MRayl, PZT about 34.
Transducer made of thin vibrating membranes over vacuum gaps, built with silicon micromachining.
Micromachined plate transducer driven by a thin piezoelectric film.
Thin-film piezoelectric used in PMUTs; CMOS-compatible.
AlN alloyed with scandium for a larger piezoelectric coefficient.
Numerical wave simulation on a grid, stepping fields forward in time.
Numerical solution of field equations on a mesh of small elements.
Simulation using the finite element method.
Stability limit on the time step of explicit wave solvers: c·Δt/Δx must stay below a constant.
Grid samples per wavelength in a simulation; too few cause numerical dispersion.
Velocity potential at a field point produced by an impulsive normal velocity of the transducer face; the pressure is ρ₀ times the time derivative of the excitation convolved with it.
Custom chip, for example the in-probe electronics of a matrix array.
Converts the amplified analog echo into samples.
Converts digital values into an analog voltage.
First receive amplifier; sets most of the system noise figure.
Amplifier whose gain changes with depth to apply TGC.
Gain that increases with echo time to offset attenuation.
Degradation of SNR through a stage, in dB.
Resolution an ADC actually delivers once noise and distortion are counted.
Reconfigurable chip used for beamforming and data handling.
Transmit supply voltage, typically tens of volts up to about ±100 V (some systems higher).
The switching transistor of pulsers and multiplexers.
The standard integrated-circuit process; CMUTs and PMUTs can be built on top of it.
Approximating derivatives by differences on a grid.
Absorbing boundary layer that stops reflections at the edge of a simulation grid.
Parabolic model of nonlinear, diffracting, absorbing sound beams.
Cardiac imaging with a probe placed in the oesophagus.
Imaging from a catheter inside a blood vessel.
Derated (0.3 dB/cm/MHz) peak rarefactional pressure in MPa divided by the square root of the acoustic working frequency in MHz; indicates the likelihood of inertial cavitation (FDA limit 1.9).
Ratio of the relevant (attenuated, bounded) acoustic power to the power that raises a model tissue by 1 °C; an exposure indicator, not a measured temperature rise.
TI for soft tissue only.
TI with bone at or near the focus.
Time integral of instantaneous intensity over one pulse.
Highest temporal-average intensity in the field; its derated value ISPTA.3 is limited by FDA to 720 mW/cm² for most applications, alongside MI ≤ 1.9.
Short for spatial-peak temporal-average intensity (ISPTA).
Safety principle: use the lowest output and shortest exposure that answer the clinical question.
Thermal dose: heating converted to the equivalent time at 43 °C.
Standards body whose standards define acoustic output measurement and safety for ultrasound.
US regulator for medical devices, including ultrasound output limits.

f: American Institute of Ultrasound in Medicine
d: Professional society that issues safety and practice statements.
Ratio, in dB, between the largest and smallest levels a system or display represents; in B-mode, the span of log-compressed values mapped from white to black.
Decomposition of a signal into complex exponentials; the continuous counterpart of the DFT.
An equation relating a function of one variable to its derivatives.
Correlation of a signal with a shifted copy of itself, as a function of the shift.
Model-order selection rule that trades goodness of fit against the number of parameters; used here to choose the AR order.
Robust fitting: models are fitted to random minimal subsets and the one with the most inliers is kept.
Viscoelastic model that adds a spring in parallel with a fractional-order element (spring-pot).
Wave solver that computes spatial derivatives with FFTs, so it needs only a few grid points per wavelength (k-Wave uses a k-space PSTD method).
Tomographic imaging with transducers surrounding the object (for example the breast), reconstructing sound speed and attenuation as well as reflectivity.
Imaging with the second harmonic generated by nonlinear propagation in tissue, which reduces clutter from near-field reverberation and sidelobes.
Therapeutic focused ultrasound that heats and ablates tissue at the focus.
MRI method that images shear waves from an external vibrator to map tissue stiffness.
Shear wave elastography method that moves the push focus faster than the shear wave speed, creating a Mach cone of shear waves.
RSNA initiative that publishes profiles for standardizing quantitative imaging measurements, including shear wave speed.
Cardiac ultrasound imaging through the chest wall.
Microscale mechanical structures made with semiconductor fabrication; CMUTs and PMUTs are MEMS devices.
Silicone rubber used for lenses and coatings; low sound speed and fairly high attenuation.
Silicone rubber cured at room temperature; the usual acoustic lens material (sound speed about 1000 m/s).
Another name for the Cramér–Rao lower bound (CRLB).
Massively parallel processor used for beamforming, FFTs and simulation.

f: European Federation of Societies for Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology
d: European professional federation that publishes clinical and safety guidelines.
Aberration-correction method from optical microscopy that iteratively estimates input and output phase corrections from the reflection matrix.
The smallest luminance change an average observer can detect under the DICOM standard viewing target; the GSDF spaces display levels in JND steps.

The DICOM curve that maps a JND index (1–1023, 0.05–4000 cd/m²) to luminance so that equal steps in input value are roughly equally visible; calibrating a monitor to it makes images look the same on different displays.
The integer value sent to the display for a pixel; the calibration lookup table maps it to luminance.
A precomputed table that maps input values to output values, e.g. a gray map, a calibration curve or a scan-conversion index table.
The hospital system that stores and displays DICOM images on reading workstations.
Maximum over minimum luminance of a display, usually including reflected ambient light (written LR′ in that case).
PW Doppler with a PRF above the single-gate depth limit, so several sample volumes are insonated at once and the depth becomes ambiguous.
(PSV − EDV)/PSV from the maximum-frequency envelope of a spectral Doppler waveform (Pourcelot).
The maximum-velocity envelope of the spectral Doppler waveform averaged over a cardiac cycle.
The intensity-weighted mean velocity averaged over a cardiac cycle; multiplied by the vessel area it estimates volume flow.
The integral of the velocity envelope over one ejection or cardiac cycle, in cm; times the area gives stroke volume.
The language the in-page demos run in; 'run in this page (JS)' marks results computed live in your browser rather than in the Octave scripts.
The reference sinusoid at the demodulation frequency that the RF signal is mixed with to shift it to baseband.
Processing of sampled signals by algorithms; also the programmable chip that runs them in real time.

f: Fastest Fourier Transform in the West
d: Widely used open-source FFT library (Frigo and Johnson) that picks a fast algorithm for each transform size; MATLAB's fft is built on it.
Factorization PA = LU into lower- and upper-triangular matrices; solving a linear system by two triangular solves is cheaper and more accurate than forming the inverse.
Krylov iterative method for least-squares problems, mathematically equivalent to CGLS but more stable; early stopping regularizes.
Least-squares fitting, as in a quadratic LSQ fit of a correlation peak or a strain estimate from an LSQ slope of displacement.
In Modules 5 and 13: the conjugate-gradient iterative solver for symmetric positive-definite systems. In Module 4: the coherent gain of a window, its mean value, which scales a tone's spectral peak.
Usually a band-pass filter, which passes a band between two cut-offs. In Module 5 it also names basis pursuit, sparse recovery by L1-norm minimization.
A filter that passes frequencies above a cut-off, such as a Doppler wall filter.
Passes frequencies above a cut-off and attenuates those below; in Doppler it is the clutter (wall) filter.
A filter that passes frequencies below a cut-off.
Subspace method that estimates directions or frequencies from the noise-subspace eigenvectors of a covariance matrix.
Data-adaptive spectral and beamforming estimator that iterates weighted least squares to refine its covariance estimate from few snapshots.
The distribution of eigenvalues of a large random (noise-only) covariance matrix; eigenvalues beyond its upper edge indicate signal.
Threshold signal strength below which a low-rank signal's eigenvalue cannot be separated from the Marchenko–Pastur noise bulk.
A direction of largest variance in the data, given by a right singular vector of the centred data matrix.
One multiplication plus one addition; the unit of arithmetic cost for filters, beamformers and matrix products.
A multiply–accumulate on complex numbers, about four real multiplications and four real additions.
The BLAS matrix-multiply routine; the operation GPUs execute most efficiently.
A range computed from data that contains the true parameter with a stated probability (e.g. 95 %) over repeated experiments.
Least squares that assumes all error is in the dependent variable; when the regressor is noisy too, the slope is biased toward zero.
Estimating statistics by repeating a simulation with random noise many times; used throughout the demos to check theory.
Standard deviation divided by the mean, often in percent; a scale-free measure of repeatability.
Variation of a signal's instantaneous frequency over time, as in a chirp.
A chirp whose sweep rate varies (slower near the band centre), shaping the spectrum to lower range sidelobes without a mismatched window.
The filter whose impulse response is the time-reversed conjugate of the expected signal; it maximizes output SNR in white noise.
Cross-correlation computed with a frequency weighting (pre-whitening), such as PHAT, before the delay peak is picked.
GCC weighting that divides the cross-spectrum by its magnitude, keeping only phase; it sharpens the peak but amplifies noisy frequencies.
Median of the absolute deviations from the median; 1.48 × MAD estimates the standard deviation robustly for Gaussian data.
Block-matching cost: the sum of squared differences between a kernel and shifted copies; minimized rather than maximized.
Optical flow measurement that tracks seeded particle patterns between frames by cross-correlation.
Sampling from a posterior distribution with a random walk whose stationary distribution is that posterior.
Joint decomposition of two matrices; it analyses general-form Tikhonov regularization with a penalty operator.
Gradient descent on the least-squares objective with a fixed step; the iteration count acts as the regularization parameter.
Stochastic-gradient adaptive filter update; also the name of the Landweber-type steepest-descent step.
Least-squares optimizer that linearizes the residual and solves with JᵀJ in place of the Hessian.
Computing exact derivatives of a program by applying the chain rule to each operation; reverse mode gives the full gradient at a small multiple of one evaluation's cost.
Classical explicit ODE integrator using four slope evaluations per step; local error scales as the fifth power of the step.
Embedded Runge–Kutta pair that compares fourth- and fifth-order solutions to adapt the step size.
Detection threshold scaled by a local noise estimate so the false-alarm probability stays fixed as the background changes.
Model-order selection criterion with a heavier penalty than AIC; more conservative for long records.
Multitaper design parameter: N samples times half-bandwidth W; about 2NW − 1 DPSS tapers are well concentrated.
Eigenvalue iteration like QR but with a lower-triangular factor; the standard method for symmetric tridiagonal matrices such as the DPSS problem.
The far-field beam pattern of the array weights alone (isotropic elements); for a uniform linear array it is the DTFT of the apodization.
A replica of the main lobe produced by spatial undersampling, when the pitch exceeds λ/(1 + |sin θ₀|) for steering angle θ₀.
The directivity of a single element; the array beam pattern is the array factor times the element factor.
Combining channel signals with delays and weights to focus on each image point.
Energy outside the main lobe of a beam pattern; its level in dB relative to the peak.
Unwanted electrical pickup from external sources; coherent across firings, so averaging does not remove it.
Approximation (Garcia et al. 2013) that treats plane-wave data as if each scatterer emitted at time zero in a medium with an adjusted speed, so seismic f–k migration applies.
Seismic term for coincident source and receiver (monostatic data), so delays are 2r/c.
Power of an interfering signal relative to the noise; adaptive nulls deepen as it rises.
Blind decomposition of data into statistically independent components; used to compress ADMIRE's model matrices for speed.
ADMIRE variant (Schlunk et al. 2021) that iterates the model fit so weak tissue next to bright targets is not shrunk away.
Sound-speed autofocus loss that compares transmit–receive pairs sharing a common midpoint, whose speckle should match when the speed map is right.

f: Quantitative Ultrasound estimation of Attenuation and Speed-Of-Sound
d: IEEE IUS 2026 challenge that scored attenuation and sound-speed estimators on shared phantom and simulated data for bias, variance, detectability and robustness to aberration.
Loss in dB between the electrical power available to a transducer and the power delivered (one-way) or received back (two-way, pulse-echo).
The matching layer next to the piezoelectric plate (highest impedance of the stack).
The second matching layer, between ML1 and the tissue or lens.
Mesh-based numerical modelling (FEM/FEA); it captures lateral modes, kerf crosstalk and lens effects that 1D models miss.
Commercial explicit time-domain finite-element code for piezoelectric transducers and wave propagation, now part of the OnScale/Ansys family.
Cloud-based successor of PZFlex for explicit finite-element transducer simulation, now part of Ansys.
Commercial multiphysics finite-element package used for coupled piezoelectric, structural and acoustic simulations.
Field simulator (McGough, Michigan State) using the fast nearfield method and time–space decomposition for fast, accurate linear pressure fields.
FOCUS technique that separates the excitation's time dependence from the spatial integrals to compute transient fields quickly.
Finite-difference stencil whose error falls as the square of the grid step; needs more points per wavelength than FD4.
Wider finite-difference stencil whose error falls as the fourth power of the grid step, giving less numerical dispersion per grid point.
Time-varying signal component; in a CMUT a small AC drive rides on the DC bias, and AC poling uses an alternating field to pole crystals.
A single number combining material or device properties to rank options, e.g. transmit or receive merit of transducer materials.
(K,Na)NbO₃, a lead-free piezoelectric ceramic studied as a PZT replacement.
(Bi₀.₅Na₀.₅)TiO₃, a lead-free piezoelectric ceramic family.
(Bi₀.₅K₀.₅)TiO₃, a lead-free piezoelectric ceramic family.
Pb(Mg₁/₃Nb₂/₃)O₃; in this course mostly shorthand for the PMN-PT single crystal.
Pb(In₁/₂Nb₁/₂)O₃; added in ternary PIN-PMN-PT crystals to raise the Curie temperature and coercive field.
PbTiO₃; its fraction (about 28–33 % in PMN-PT) places the crystal near the morphotropic phase boundary, where coupling peaks.
Wafer with a thin silicon device layer on a buried oxide over a handle wafer; in wafer-bonded CMUTs the device layer becomes the membrane.
The oxide layer of an SOI wafer between the device layer and the handle.
The metal interconnect layers of a CMOS chip, built after the transistors; CMUTs can be fabricated on top of them.
Plasma etch that cuts deep, near-vertical features in silicon, e.g. PMUT cavities and through-wafer vias.
Growing thick oxide only in selected areas; used in some CMUT processes to define the gap and posts.
Microscope that images surfaces with a focused electron beam at nanometre resolution.
Board with copper traces that carries and connects electronic components.
Cardiac imaging from a catheter placed inside the heart chambers.
Level in dB relative to the largest signal an ADC can represent without clipping; ADC SNR is usually quoted this way.
Voltage level 20·log₁₀(V / 1 V); −96 dBV is about 16 µV.
Level of a harmonic or spurious tone in dB relative to the fundamental.
MS/s means 10⁶ samples per second, the unit of ADC and oscilloscope sampling rates.
Integrated circuit combining LNA, VGA, anti-aliasing filter and ADC (often with a CW mixer) for 8–16 receive channels.
The smallest step an ADC resolves: the full-scale range divided by 2 to the number of bits.
Power of a test tone over all noise and distortion power; ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76 dB)/6.02 dB.
A chip carrying many transistors and passive parts, such as an analog front end.
Serial digital interface standard used to stream ADC samples to the FPGA.
Serial interface standard for high-speed ADC and DAC data links, carrying several channels per multi-gigabit lane.
Serial point-to-point bus linking acquisition hardware to host memory and GPUs; bandwidth scales with generation and lane count (×8, ×16).
Shaping a waveform's average by varying the width of fixed-level pulses; lets switching pulsers approximate apodized or tapered transmits.
Pulser drive that returns to 0 V between positive and negative half-cycles (three-level drive).
Choosing the switching instants of a multi-level pulse so that chosen harmonics cancel.
Non-volatile memory; in a probe it stores identification and calibration data.
DTU research scanner with 1024 channels that stores all channel data for offline synthetic-aperture processing.
University of Leeds open research scanner platform with FPGA-based transmit and receive.
Short for spatial-peak pulse-average intensity (ISPPA): the highest intensity averaged over the pulse duration; ISPPA.3 is the derated value.
Subscript for the maximum over the field, as in ISPTA.
Subscript for an average over the pulse repetition period, as in ISPTA.
Subscript for an average over the pulse duration, as in ISPPA or IPA.3.
Fraction of time the transducer is transmitting: pulse duration times PRF.
Obstetric (pregnancy) imaging; output guidance is stricter for OB scans, especially after 10 weeks when fetal bone forms.
Reference date for gestational age; thermal-index guidance uses weeks after the LMP.
AIUM/NEMA standard (NEMA UD 3) for real-time on-screen display of MI and TI; the basis of FDA Track 3.
NEMA ultrasound standards: UD 2 for acoustic output measurement and UD 3, the Output Display Standard for MI and TI.
UK professional society whose safety guidelines give MI and TI thresholds and scanning-time advice.

f: International Transcranial Ultrasonic Stimulation Safety and Standards consortium
d: Expert consortium that publishes consensus safety recommendations for transcranial ultrasound, including use of the cranial thermal index.
Maximum of the time–intensity curve above baseline; a CEUS perfusion parameter.
Maximum slope of the rising part of the time–intensity curve.
In contrast imaging, the area under the time–intensity curve (a perfusion parameter); in detection studies, the area under the ROC curve.
Contrast sequence combining amplitude and polarity changes (e.g. +1 and −½) whose sum cancels linear echoes but keeps even-order echoes and odd-order echoes in the fundamental band.
A phospholipid used, with DSPC, in microbubble shells.
Highest velocity of the maximum-frequency Doppler envelope during systole.
Velocity of the maximum-frequency Doppler envelope at the end of diastole.
Vector-flow method that shapes the receive apodization to create a lateral oscillation in the PSF, so lateral velocity can be estimated.
Spectral Doppler estimator using a Capon (minimum-variance) filter bank to sharpen spectra from short ensembles.
Adaptive spectral Doppler estimator using a bank of matched filters to resolve spectra from few samples.
Clutter power relative to blood-signal power, in dB; it sets the stopband attenuation the wall filter needs.
Imaging of brain activity through blood-volume changes measured by ultrafast power Doppler.

f: sample volume (or vertically polarized shear wave)
d: In Doppler (Module 29): the range-gated region the spectrum comes from. In anisotropic elastography (Module 30): the vertically polarized shear wave, coupled to the tensile modulus.
In transversely isotropic tissue such as muscle, the shear wave polarized in the fibre plane; its speed depends on angle to the fibres.
Viscoelastic model of a spring and dashpot in parallel; it predicts shear-wave speed growing without bound with frequency.
Cross-correlation time-delay estimate, e.g. of shear-wave arrival.
Shear-wave method that reports one speed from a small ROI after a push, rather than a 2D map.
US society whose consensus statements, e.g. on liver elastography and carotid stenosis, set clinical criteria.
Advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis without decompensation; in the SRU consensus, a shear-wave liver stiffness above about 13 kPa suggests it.
Hepatic venous pressure gradient of 10 mmHg or more; in the SRU consensus, a shear-wave liver stiffness above about 17 kPa makes it probable.
Recording of the heart's electrical activity, used to gate acquisitions to the cardiac cycle.
Spread between the 25th and 75th percentiles; IQR/median ≤ 30 % is the usual reliability check for liver stiffness.
Mean over standard deviation of the strain estimate in a uniform region.
Tomographic imaging of nuclear magnetic resonance signals; MR elastography uses it to image shear waves.
As in MR elastography, which images shear waves with MRI.
X-ray tomographic imaging; in aberration correction, CT gives prior sound-speed and density maps of bone.
ULM used to measure activity-driven blood-flow changes at microvascular scale.
Centroid localization: the intensity-weighted mean position inside a small box.
Localization that finds the point closest to all lines along the local intensity gradients.
Localization by a three-point Gaussian (log-parabola) fit to the peak.
Localization by finding the peak of a cubically interpolated (upsampled) image.
Super-resolution method that recovers microbubble positions by sparse recovery rather than isolating single bubbles.

f: Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine
d: The standard (NEMA PS3) for medical image files, networking and display, including ultrasound image objects, region calibration and the grayscale display function.
The DICOM standard as published by NEMA; PS3.n is Part n, e.g. PS3.3 (information objects) and PS3.14 (Grayscale Standard Display Function).
DICOM specification of the attributes an object, such as an ultrasound image, must or may contain.
DICOM photometric interpretation for grayscale images in which the minimum value is displayed as black.
Colour encoding with one value per primary; colour ultrasound stored as RGB takes three times the data of MONOCHROME2.
Standard colour space (IEC 61966-2-1) with defined primaries, white point and transfer curve; the default for consumer displays.
DICOM colour encoding with one luminance and two colour-difference channels; used with JPEG, where chroma can be subsampled.
Body that defines colorimetry, including the XYZ colour space and the CIELAB lightness L*.
Approximately perceptually uniform colour space; L* is lightness, used to judge whether a colour map changes evenly.
Reduced ability to distinguish some colours (roughly 8 % of men, mostly red–green); colour maps should stay readable for it.
Display that modulates a backlight with liquid-crystal cells; luminance and contrast change with viewing angle.
Emissive display technology whose pixels emit light and can switch fully off, giving a very low black level.
Image compression standard; lossy JPEG quantizes 8 × 8 block DCT coefficients and can remove fine speckle and edge detail.
Real-valued Fourier-related transform; the block transform inside JPEG compression.
Planned, periodic tests (display, probe or array checks) that verify a system still meets its specifications.

f: American Association of Physicists in Medicine
d: Society whose task-group reports (e.g. TG18, Report 270) define display quality-control tests.
AAPM report (2005) and test patterns for assessing medical display performance: luminance response, uniformity, resolution and noise.
Professional body that, with AAPM and SIIM, publishes the technical standard for electronic display of medical images.

f: Society for Imaging Informatics in Medicine
d: Professional society for imaging informatics; co-author of the ACR–AAPM–SIIM display standard.
US association that publishes DICOM (as NEMA PS3) and the ultrasound UD standards.
DICOM modality code for ultrasound, as in the US Image and US Region Calibration modules.
10·log₁₀ of the squared peak value over the mean squared error to a reference image; misleading for speckle, which has no clean reference.
Similarity measure combining local luminance, contrast and structure against a reference (Wang et al. 2004); like PSNR, it misleads for speckle.
Mapping intensities through their cumulative distribution so the output histogram is approximately flat.
Histogram equalization in tiles with a clip limit on each histogram, blended between tiles, to raise local contrast without excessive noise amplification.
Probability that a random variable is at or below a given value.
Diffusion filter (Yu and Acton 2002) whose diffusion coefficient follows a local speckle statistic, smoothing homogeneous speckle while stopping at edges.
Denoiser that replaces each pixel by a weighted average of pixels whose surrounding patches look similar, wherever they are in the image.
NLM variant for ultrasound (Coupé et al. 2009) whose patch distance is derived from a speckle noise model.
Denoiser (Dabov et al. 2007) that groups similar patches into 3D stacks and shrinks them jointly in a transform domain.
Volumetric extension of BM3D (Maggioni et al. 2013) that groups similar 3D cubes.
Best linear estimator in the mean-squared sense; computed from local mean and variance it gives the Lee and Kuan speckle filters.
Squared mean over variance of intensity in a homogeneous region: 1 for fully developed speckle, larger after averaging or despeckling.
Image of a sharp step edge; its 10–90 % width and its derivative (the LSF) measure resolution.
Image of a thin line, equal to the derivative of the edge spread function; its FWHM is a resolution measure.
Volume rendering that shows the largest voxel value along each ray; good for bright sparse targets such as contrast-filled vessels.
The mapping from voxel value to colour and opacity in volume rendering.
Curve of true-positive rate against false-positive rate as a decision threshold varies; its area (AUC) summarizes detectability.
Reader-study design in which several readers interpret the same cases, so conclusions generalize over both readers and cases.
Radar imaging from a moving antenna; its speckle filters (Lee, Kuan, Frost) were adopted by ultrasound.
Machine learning with many-layer neural networks trained on data.
A generator trained against a discriminator; as a loss it can create realistic-looking but false image detail.
Inputs unlike the training data (other probes, sites or patients), on which learned filters can fail silently.
Interferometric optical imaging with micrometre resolution; it shares fully developed speckle with ultrasound.

Two meanings: artificial intelligence (learned algorithms in device software, e.g. an AI view classifier), and FDA's additional-information request (AI letter) that puts a 510(k) on hold for up to 180 days.
In 510(k) review: the finding that a device has the same intended use as a legally marketed predicate and is as safe and effective. In statistics (Module 5): the standard deviation of an estimate.
510(k) decision that a device is not substantially equivalent to its predicate; it then needs a De Novo request, a PMA or a new 510(k).

In physics: the International System of Units (metre, kilogram, second). In 510(k) review (Module 36): FDA's day-60 Substantive Interaction, which either requests additional information or continues interactive review.
Codified U.S. federal rules; Title 21 covers FDA, e.g. 21 CFR 892.1550 classifies ultrasound Doppler imaging systems and Part 820 holds the QMSR.

f: Center for Devices and Radiological Health
d: The FDA centre that regulates medical devices and radiation-emitting products, including ultrasound.
Ultrasonic pulsed Doppler imaging system (21 CFR 892.1550, Class II); the usual primary code of a general-purpose scanner.
Ultrasonic pulsed echo imaging system (21 CFR 892.1560, Class II).
Diagnostic ultrasonic transducer (21 CFR 892.1570, Class II).
Automated radiological image processing software (21 CFR 892.2050, Class II); often listed for software and AI functions of an imaging system.
Software that marks image regions likely to contain a lesion for the reader to review.
U.S. user-fee agreements that fund device review and set FDA performance goals, e.g. MDUFA V: a 510(k) decision within 90 FDA days for 95 % of submissions.
MDUFA metric: calendar days from receipt to the 510(k) decision, including time on hold, unlike FDA days.
FDA's interactive submission template, required for 510(k)s since 1 October 2023; incomplete eSTARs are put on hold at technical screening.
FDA's voluntary electronic template, analogous to eSTAR, for Pre-Submissions and other Q-Submission types.
FDA acceptance review that could reject an incomplete 510(k); eSTAR submissions get technical screening instead.
FDA's most stringent route, for Class III devices, requiring valid scientific evidence (usually clinical) of safety and effectiveness.
FDA approval that lets an unapproved significant-risk device be used in a U.S. clinical study.
Plan authorized in a marketing submission that specifies future device changes (e.g. AI retraining) and how they will be validated, so they need no new submission.
The organization's documented processes for design, production and post-market activities; ISO 13485 in the EU and the QMSR in the U.S.
FDA's 21 CFR 820, effective 2 February 2026, which incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference and replaced the Quality System Regulation.
FDA's former inspection method under the Quality System Regulation, retired when the QMSR took effect.
Records showing a device was developed under design controls; under ISO 13485 and the QMSR it is the design and development file.
QMS process that investigates nonconformities and complaints, fixes their causes and prevents recurrence.
IEC 62304 term for off-the-shelf software not developed under the manufacturer's process; it must be listed, specified and risk-assessed.
List of the software components (commercial, open-source, off-the-shelf) in a device; FDA requires it for cyber devices.
How users interact with a device; FDA expects a use-related risk analysis and, if critical tasks exist, validation testing (IEC 62366-1).
Applying knowledge of human abilities and limits to device design and validation; documented in the HFE/usability engineering report.
Analysis of user tasks, possible use errors and their harms that identifies the critical tasks for human-factors validation.
Device software, documented and verified per IEC 62304 and FDA's software guidance.
The controls and displays through which a user operates the device.
As in the FDA 510(k), recall and MAUDE databases.
FDA program in which accredited labs test to eligible standards (e.g. the IEC 60601 series) and issue summary reports reviewers can rely on.

f: Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience
d: FDA database of medical device reports (MDRs); a source of failure modes, not of failure rates.
FDA database that links premarket clearances, device reports (MDRs) and recalls by product code.
FDA's recall database (cfRES in its web address); each record gives the product, the FDA-determined cause and the corrective action.
FDA's public data interface (web API and downloads) for device clearances, recalls and adverse-event reports.
Standards body behind, e.g., ISO 13485 (quality management) and ISO 14971 (risk management) used in device regulation.
U.S. body that accredits standards developers and designates American National Standards, e.g. ANSI/AAMI ES60601-1.

f: Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation
d: U.S. standards organization; publishes national adoptions such as ANSI/AAMI ES60601-1 and technical reports such as TIR69.
Ability of equipment to work in its electromagnetic environment without causing or suffering interference; tested to IEC 60601-1-2.
First amendment to an IEC or ISO standard edition; a test plan must cite the edition plus amendment it uses.
Second amendment to an IEC or ISO standard edition.
Union of European states whose Medical Device Regulation (MDR) sets the route to the CE mark.

f: Medical Device Regulation (EU); medical device report (U.S.)
d: In EU context: Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on classification, technical documentation and CE marking. In U.S. postmarket context: a report of a death, serious injury or malfunction under 21 CFR 803, stored in MAUDE.

f: In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation
d: Regulation (EU) 2017/746, the IVD counterpart of the MDR.
A device that examines specimens taken from the body, such as blood tests.
Family of video coding standards (MPEG-2, H.264/MPEG-4 AVC, H.265) that DICOM allows for lossy cine storage.
Routine checks that a device or display still meets its specification, as in the AAPM TG18-QC test pattern.
Short for the transmit side or transmit event of an imaging sequence (as in Tx apodization or Tx focus).
Short for the receive side of an imaging sequence (as in Rx aperture or Rx beamforming).
Domain of the 2D Fourier transform over time and array position; f-k (Stolt) migration images by remapping this spectrum.
Doppler index: peak systolic velocity divided by end-diastolic velocity.
Focal depth divided by aperture width; sets lateral resolution (about λ·F#) and the receive aperture growth with depth.
DMAS followed by a band-pass around 2f₀ to keep the second-harmonic-like component of the pairwise products.
Temporal-average intensity averaged over the beam cross-section; lower than ISPTA.
MRI-based fraction of liver signal from fat; the usual reference standard for ultrasound steatosis measures.
The region of tissue the image covers (depth × width or sector angle).
A detection declared where no true target exists; traded against missed detections by the threshold.
Images formed per second; limited by depth, lines or transmits per frame and processing.
Polymer brush grafted to lipid microbubble shells to stabilize them and reduce clearance.
Flexural guided wave in a plate; its dispersion is used in shear-wave elastography of thin tissues.
Array factor of the subarray centres in a micro-beamformed array; its grating lobes are set by the subarray pitch.
Beam pattern of one subarray; multiplies the coarse array factor in a micro-beamformed array.
10⁹ bytes; used for channel-data volumes and memory sizes.

f: Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2022
d: U.S. law whose section 3308 added FD&C Act section 515C, the statutory basis for predetermined change control plans (PCCPs).
FDA, Health Canada and MHRA guiding principles (2021) for developing machine-learning-enabled medical devices.

f: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
d: The UK regulator for medicines and medical devices.
FDA database of device-identifier records that labelers submit under 21 CFR 830.
Static part of a UDI that identifies the labeler and the model or version; the EU's Basic UDI-DI is the model-level key in EUDAMED.
The manufacturer's signed EU statement that a device meets the MDR (Article 19, Annex IV).
EUDAMED identifier assigned to a registered economic operator.
AMA code set used for billing U.S. procedures; Category I codes for established services, Category III for emerging ones.
Platform software of a scanner or workstation; OS updates are treated as software changes in FDA's change guidance.
Use without a prescription; moving a device from prescription to OTC use is an intended-use change.
Weight divided by height squared (kg/m²); a key covariate of ultrasound image quality in subgroup analyses.
EU board under the AI Act; issues guidance jointly with the MDCG on AI medical devices.
Liver stiffness method that tracks a shear wave launched by a mechanical vibrator (the FibroScan principle), reported in kPa.
Inflammatory form of metabolic fatty liver disease (formerly NASH); a key target for elastography and attenuation imaging.

f: World Federation for Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology
d: International federation that publishes ultrasound guidelines, e.g. on liver elastography and contrast ultrasound.
Region just below the aortic valve; its diameter and Doppler VTI give stroke volume and, with the continuity equation, valve area.
Effective orifice area of the aortic valve, usually computed with the continuity equation from LVOT diameter and two VTIs.

f: North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial
d: Trial whose angiographic method of grading carotid stenosis underlies the Doppler velocity criteria.
Professional society that publishes echocardiography guidelines and measurement conventions.
European society that co-publishes echocardiography guidelines with the ASE.

f: Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System
d: ACR system for categorizing liver observations in patients at risk of hepatocellular carcinoma; a CEUS version defines enhancement-based categories.
Enhancement in the arterial phase greater than the surrounding liver; a major LI-RADS feature.
Primary liver cancer; the main target of LI-RADS categorization.
Quantitative contrast ultrasound: time–intensity curves are fitted to derive perfusion parameters.

f: Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement
d: The JCGM/ISO reference method for combining measurement uncertainties; used for tolerance and test-limit budgets.
Structured review of how each part or process step can fail, its effect and its detectability; used in design and process risk management.
Hysteresis loop of a ferroelectric's polarization versus applied field; gives the coercive field and remanent polarization.
IEEE conference where integrated ultrasound front-end and probe ASICs are often first reported.
FDA eSTAR version for devices other than in vitro diagnostics.
EU group of national authorities that issues MDR guidance documents (MDCG yyyy-n), e.g. on classification, clinical evaluation and PSURs.
Medium-risk class under MDR Annex VIII; diagnostic ultrasound is IIa by Rule 10, so a notified body must assess the QMS and technical documentation.
Higher-risk class under MDR Annex VIII; Rule 10 puts devices for monitoring vital parameters, where variations could mean immediate danger, in IIb.
Organization designated by an EU member state to assess conformity of Class IIa and higher devices (QMS audit and technical-documentation review).

f: New Approach Notified and Designated Organisations
d: European Commission database listing notified bodies and the MDR scope each is designated for.
Mark showing conformity with EU legislation; for Class IIa and higher devices it requires a notified-body certificate.
European version of a standard (e.g. EN 60601-1); harmonised ENs give a presumption of conformity with the MDR.
MDR Annex I requirements every device must meet; the technical documentation shows conformity, usually in a GSPR checklist citing standards and evidence.
The MDR Annex II and III file (description, GSPR checklist, risk, verification, clinical evaluation, PMS) that the notified body assesses.
Document that appraises clinical data (own studies, literature, equivalence) to show conformity with the safety and performance requirements.
The manufacturer's system for collecting and analysing data on devices in use and feeding it back into risk management and design.
MDR activity that collects clinical data on a CE-marked device in use to confirm its safety and performance over its life.
MDR Article 86 report of post-market data and benefit–risk conclusions: at least every two years for Class IIa, yearly for IIb and III.
EU term for software with a medical purpose, standalone or driving a device; classified by MDR Rule 11.
System of device identifiers on labels, held in GUDID (U.S.) and EUDAMED (EU), that traces a device model and production lot.
EU database for actor and device (UDI) registration, certificates, vigilance and clinical investigations.
Team-NB documents describing what notified bodies expect, e.g. in technical documentation.
Labeling that tells users how to operate the device safely, with indications, warnings and, for ultrasound, acoustic-output information.
Hospital unit for critically ill patients; continuous monitoring there can raise an ultrasound device's EU class.
Square root of the mean of the squared values; for a zero-mean signal, its standard deviation.
Usually maximum likelihood: the estimate that makes the observed data most probable (see MLE). In 'ML texts' (Module 13) it means machine learning.
Standards body; ASTM E1065 specifies how ultrasonic transducers are characterized (centre frequency, bandwidth).
Radiology society that hosts QIBA, the Quantitative Imaging Biomarkers Alliance.
An early heartbeat triggered in the ventricles; reported as a contrast-agent bioeffect at elevated MI.
